title: Narrative Devices in Classic Fiction
text:
Classic novelists often relied on an omniscient narrator who could reveal the thoughts of every character. This technique gave readers a broad view of the story, but it also distanced them from any single perspective. Foreshadowing was another common device, allowing authors to hint at future events without revealing them outright. Such hints built suspense and encouraged careful rereading.

Irony, by contrast, depended on the gap between what characters believed and what readers already understood. When a character spoke with confidence about a situation that the narrator had already exposed as false, the effect was both humorous and unsettling. Writers who mastered these devices could shape a reader's judgment with remarkable subtlety.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what did the omniscient narrator allow readers to know?
options: The future of the author's career
The price of the printed book

questions.text: According to paragraph two, what did irony depend on?
options: The gap between what characters believed and what readers understood

questions.text: What can be inferred about the effect of foreshadowing?
options: It encouraged readers to reread and anticipate what might come
It removed all suspense from the story
It forced readers to skip difficult passages

questions.text: What can be inferred about writers who mastered these devices?
options: They wrote only for professional critics
They could influence how readers judged characters without stating it directly
They preferred short stories to novels

vocabulary.definition: knowing everything, especially about the thoughts of all characters
a hint about events that will happen later in the story
a feeling of uncertainty and excitement about what will happen next
the quality of being delicate, indirect and hard to notice

paragraph_translations: Romancistas clássicos muitas vezes recorriam a um narrador onisciente, capaz de revelar os pensamentos de todos os personagens. Essa técnica oferecia ao leitor uma visão ampla da história, mas também o afastava de qualquer perspectiva única. A prefiguração era outro recurso comum, permitindo que os autores insinuassem eventos futuros sem revelá-los abertamente. Essas pistas criavam suspense e incentivavam uma releitura atenta.

A ironia, em contraste, dependia da distância entre o que os personagens acreditavam e o que os leitores já entendiam. Quando um personagem falava com confiança sobre uma situação que o narrador já havia exposto como falsa, o efeito era ao mesmo tempo cômico e inquietante. Escritores que dominavam esses recursos podiam moldar o julgamento do leitor com notável sutileza.
